questions.q: On which stretch of the Indian coast did the Bene Israel settle, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Konkan coast, just south of Mumbai. The Malabar coast is where Syriac Christians landed, the Gujarat coast is where the Parsis arrived, and Kochi is where a later Jewish group settled.
o: The Konkan coast, just south of Mumbai
The Malabar coast, in present-day Kerala
The western coast, in present-day Gujarat
The coast near Cochin, now called Kochi

questions.q: According to some scholars, how did the first group of the Bene Israel come to be on the Indian coast?
questions.a: Their ship was caught in a storm and wrecked near the coast, and the survivors settled. They did not come as invited traders, soldiers or monks fleeing Nalanda.
o: Their ship was caught in a storm and wrecked near the coast
The Raja of Kochi invited them to open a trading post on the coast
They marched in as soldiers of a Maharaja's army and then stayed on
They fled the destruction of Nalanda and sailed west across the sea

questions.q: Which of these is NOT said in the chapter about the Jews who settled near Cochin?
questions.a: The chapter says the land was granted free of cost, so a heavy payment is false. The 12th to 19th century arrival, the persecution they faced and the synagogue are all in the chapter.
o: The Raja made them pay a heavy price for the land
They arrived between the 12th and 19th centuries
They had again faced persecution in their own countries
They built a synagogue on the land they were given

questions.q: Which word in the chapter stands for the place where Jews hold religious services and ceremonies such as weddings?
questions.a: Synagogue is the place of worship. The Torah is the religious book, a heretic is a person with contrary beliefs, and Udvada is the Parsi sacred-fire town.
o: Synagogue
Torah
Heretic
Udvada

questions.q: Farhan reads that a ship carrying some Jews broke up in a storm; the survivors reached a shore, lost their holy books, yet still recited a prayer that there is only one God. Which community is he reading about?
questions.a: This is the Bene Israel story. The Kochi group built a synagogue after arriving later, the Parsis came from Persia to Gujarat, and the Syriac Christians travelled east along trade routes.
o: The Bene Israel of the Konkan coast
The Jews who settled near Kochi and built a synagogue
The Parsis who sailed across the sea to Gujarat
The Syriac Christians who reached Malabar by land

questions.q: Josh tells his Class 7 friends that his great-grandfather was not born into a Jewish family but joined the faith. Going by the chapter's note on 'Jews', what is the right reply?
questions.a: The chapter says a Jew may be identified by descent from Jewish ancestry or through conversion, so Josh's great-grandfather counts. The other replies add conditions the note does not state.
o: He can still be called a Jew, as conversion is one way of being identified
He cannot be called a Jew, as only descent from Jewish ancestors counts
He can be called a Jew only if the family lives near Kochi
He cannot be called a Jew, as the term applies only to people of ancient Israel

questions.q:
Read the statements about Jews in India.
1. Jews sought sanctuary in India in a single wave, after which no group came again.
2. The Bene Israel lost their holy books but remembered a prayer saying there is only one God.
3. Some Jewish groups reached India between the 12th and 19th centuries, again facing persecution.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 1 is false because the chapter says Jews sought sanctuary in several waves.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Bene Israel grew to be the largest Jewish community in India, numbering over 25,000 shortly after independence.
Reason (R): A Jew may be identified through descent from Jewish ancestry or through conversion.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but how a Jew is identified says nothing about why the Bene Israel community grew, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) State the words in which the Raja of Kochi described how long the land grant would last. (b) Why do those words matter to the future of the community that received the land?
questions.a: (a) 'As long as the world, sun, and moon endure'. (b) They promise the shelter will last without limit, so the community could build a synagogue and practise its faith securely while becoming part of Indian society.
s: Part (a): quotes the phrase 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure'
Part (b): uses (a): the promise has no end, so the community could settle, build and practise its faith securely

questions.q: (a) Name the community that lost its holy books after reaching the Konkan coast. (b) What did its members remember that kept their faith alive?
questions.a: (a) The Bene Israel. (b) Their prayer, which says there is only one God.
s: Part (a): names the Bene Israel
Part (b): the prayer saying there is only one God

questions.q: What is a synagogue? Why did the synagogue built on the Raja's land matter to the Jews of Kochi?
questions.a: A synagogue is a place of worship for Jews where religious services and special ceremonies like weddings are held. It enabled them to practise their faith even as they became part of Indian society.
s: Defines synagogue as a Jewish place of worship (services, ceremonies such as weddings)
Explains it let them practise their faith while becoming part of Indian society

questions.q: The Grade 6 book called many Indians 'migrants' because they do not live near their birthplace. In what way are the migrants of this chapter 'another type'?
questions.a: They did not move within India. They came from other parts of the world and settled here, adding another dimension to India's diversity.
s: They came from outside India, not from within it
They settled here and added another dimension to diversity

questions.q: Distinguish the arrival of the Bene Israel from that of the Jewish groups who settled near Cochin, on the basis of time and manner.
questions.a: The Bene Israel came around 175 BCE according to some scholars, surviving a shipwreck. The Cochin groups came much later, between the 12th and 19th centuries, and the Raja granted them land.
s: Bene Israel: around 175 BCE by some scholars, shipwreck survivors
Cochin groups: 12th to 19th centuries, given land by the Raja

questions.q: Rhea says, 'Jews came to India only once, so every Indian Jew descends from the Bene Israel.' Evaluate her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: She is wrong. The chapter says Jews sought sanctuary in several waves. Groups arrived much later, between the 12th and 19th centuries, and settled near Cochin. The Bene Israel were the largest community, not the only one.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong, with the word 'only once' challenged
Evidence: the chapter speaks of several waves
Evidence: later groups settled near Cochin, so the Bene Israel were not the only Jews

questions.q: Swami Vivekananda said in 1893 that he was proud to belong to a nation that had sheltered the persecuted. Using the story of Indian Jews, give three points that support his pride.
questions.a: Persecution elsewhere forced Jews to flee, and India let them practise their faith without fear. The Bene Israel started a new life and grew into the largest Jewish community. The Raja of Kochi gave land free of cost and the Jews built a synagogue.
s: Jews were forced to flee persecution in various countries and India let them practise their faith without fear
Bene Israel started a new life and became the largest Jewish community
Kochi Raja's free land and the synagogue

questions.q: Write a three-line letter that a Jewish settler near Cochin might send to relatives abroad, explaining why the family has decided to stay. Each line must use one fact from the chapter.
questions.a: Any three accurate lines, for example: the Raja has given us land free of cost; we have built a synagogue and pray as before; the grant lasts as long as the world, sun and moon endure.
s: Line 1 uses a correct chapter fact such as the free land
Line 2 uses a different correct fact such as the synagogue
Line 3 uses a third correct chapter fact, different from lines 1 and 2

questions.q: 'India proved to be a safe haven where Jews could practise their faith without fear.' Justify this statement with the stories of the Bene Israel and the Jews of Kochi.
questions.a: Persecution in various countries forced Jews to flee. The Bene Israel survived a shipwreck, started a new life, kept their prayer and became the largest Jewish community. The Raja of Kochi gave land free of cost for as long as the world, sun and moon endure, and the Jews built a synagogue.
s: Persecution elsewhere forced Jews to flee
Bene Israel: new life, prayer kept, largest community of over 25,000
Kochi: free land and a synagogue to practise their faith

questions.q: Compare how the Bene Israel and the Jews of Kochi came to India and settled, and analyse what the two stories together show about India.
questions.a: The Bene Israel arrived after a shipwreck on the Konkan coast, survivors who started a new life and kept their prayer. The Kochi Jews arrived much later, between the 12th and 19th centuries, again facing persecution, and received land free of cost. Both kept their faith while living in India, and Kochi's Jews became part of Indian society. Together they show India as a safe haven over centuries.
s: Bene Israel: shipwreck on the Konkan coast, survivors started a new life
Kochi Jews: arrived 12th-19th centuries, again facing persecution, given land by the Raja
Contrast in time and manner (shipwreck survivors versus later groups given land)
Analysis: faith kept while becoming part of society, India a safe haven across centuries

questions.q:
Class 7C in a Pune school plans an exhibition 'India as a Safe Home' on Indian Jews. The teacher must choose the opening panel: Panel X shows the Raja of Kochi's land grant; Panel Y shows the synagogue built on that land. A visiting parent asks whether Jews in India had to give up their identity to live here.
(a) On which coast did the Bene Israel settle, and how did the first group come to be there? (b) On what terms, and for how long, did the Raja of Kochi grant the land? (c) Answer the parent's question using the chapter. (d) Which panel, X or Y, better shows the integration of Jews into Indian society? Choose one and justify.
questions.a: (a) The Konkan coast, just south of Mumbai; their ship was wrecked in a storm and the survivors settled. (b) Free of cost, 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure'. (c) No; the synagogue enabled them to practise their faith even as they became part of Indian society. (d) Panel Y is better supported: the chapter ties the synagogue directly to keeping the faith while becoming part of society, whereas Panel X shows only the welcome given by the ruler. Panel X is acceptable only if the student argues that the grant came first and made the synagogue possible.
s: Part (a): Konkan coast and shipwreck
Part (b): free of cost, 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure'
Part (c): identity kept (faith practised) while becoming part of society
Part (d): a panel chosen with the trade-off stated (ruler's welcome versus community's own faith and integration) using chapter evidence

questions.q:
A quiz club in a Kolkata school reads a line spoken in Chicago in 1893: 'I am proud to belong to a nation which has sheltered the persecuted and the refugees of all religions and all nations of the Earth.' The club plans a poster with this line and needs one more panel, either the Bene Israel's population of over 25,000 shortly after independence or the Raja of Kochi's gift of land.
(a) Who spoke these words? (b) Name the Jewish group the speaker said took refuge in Southern India. (c) What did the community build on the land the Raja gave, and what does the grant's wording 'as long as the world, sun, and moon endure' tell you about the shelter? (d) The key word of the line is 'sheltered'. Which panel is the more direct proof of it, and what does the other panel prove instead?
questions.a: (a) Swami Vivekananda, at the World Parliament of Religions. (b) The remnant of the Israelites, the Jews. (c) A synagogue; the wording shows the shelter was meant to last without limit. (d) The land grant is the direct proof of sheltering, since a host gave land free of cost. The 25,000 figure proves what followed: the community survived and grew over time.
s: Part (a): Swami Vivekananda
Part (b): the Jews as the remnant of the Israelites
Part (c): a synagogue, and the shelter was lasting
Part (d): land grant as direct proof of sheltering; population figure shows later growth

questions.q: Zoroastrianism was the state religion of which empire, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The Sassanid Empire of the 3rd to 7th centuries. The Roman Empire is where Syriac Christians were called heretics, while Sanjan and Israel are a kingdom and an ancient land.
o: The Sassanid Empire
The Roman Empire
The Kingdom of Sanjan
The Kingdom of Israel

questions.q: What little did the Parsis carry with them when they left Persia, besides their hope of finding a safe home?
questions.a: Their sacred fire. The Torah belongs to the Jews, the jug of milk figures in the Sanjan legend, and Sanskrit manuscripts were carried by monks to Tibet.
o: Their sacred fire
The Torah
A jug of milk
Sanskrit manuscripts

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT named in the chapter as a form of persecution faced by Zoroastrians after the fall of the Sassanid Empire?
questions.a: Being sold into slavery to foreign traders is the story of the Siddis, not the Zoroastrians. Forced conversions, the jizya tax and the destruction of fire temples are all in the chapter.
o: Being sold into slavery to foreign traders
Forced conversions to Islam under the new rulers
Religious taxes called jizya imposed on them
Destruction of their sacred fire temples in Persia

questions.q: In the 4th century CE a group that worships in the Syriac language is called heretic by one empire and suspected of helping that empire's enemy by another. What does the chapter say such groups did?
questions.a: Some travelled eastward along trade routes to the Malabar coast. Sailing across the Arabian Sea to Gujarat is the Parsi route, crossing the Himalaya is the Tibetan route and Agra was the Armenian settlement.
o: Travelled eastward along trade routes to the Malabar coast
Sailed across the Arabian Sea to the coast of Gujarat in boats
Crossed the Himalaya and took refuge at Dharamshala in the north
Settled at Agra with the emperor's leave to build a church

questions.q: In a class play of the Sanjan legend, Jivan is the Raja and holds up a jug brimming with milk. What should the Parsi wise man do to follow the legend?
questions.a: He should dissolve a spoon of sugar in the milk without letting it spill. Pouring out milk would defeat the point, since the jug stands for a kingdom that is full.
o: Dissolve a spoon of sugar in the milk without letting it spill
Pour out half the milk to make room for the new visitors
Add more milk until the jug overflows on to the floor
Hold up a second jug of sugar and offer it to the Raja in exchange for land

questions.q:
Read the statements about Zoroastrianism.
1. It was founded by the prophet Zarathushtra in Central Asia.
2. It is based on the worship of one God, Ahura Mazda, and was founded by Raja Jadi Rana of Sanjan.
3. India today has the largest population of followers of Zoroastrianism in the world.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the faith was founded by the prophet Zarathushtra; Jadi Rana was the king of Sanjan who gave the Parsis a secure place.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Some Syriac Christians travelled eastward along trade routes to the Malabar coast.
Reason (R): In the Persian Empire they were suspected of secretly helping the Romans, who were enemies of Persia, and were persecuted.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the persecution described in R is why they left, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Groups of Zoroastrians sailed across the Arabian Sea and reached the western coast of Gujarat.
Reason (R): Old Avestan and Vedic Sanskrit share many word roots and grammatical features.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the shared word roots say nothing about why the Parsis sailed to Gujarat, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Zarathushtra  2. Jadi Rana  3. Udvada  4. Syriac Christians
Column B: a. King of Sanjan who gave the Parsis a secure place  b. Prophet who founded Zoroastrianism  c. Place where the ancient sacred fire still burns  d. Christians who used an ancient language in worship and reached Malabar
questions.a: Zarathushtra founded Zoroastrianism; Jadi Rana ruled Sanjan; the sacred fire burns at Udvada; Syriac Christians reached Malabar. The wrong options swap the king with the prophet or the place with the community.

questions.q: (a) Give the reason for which the Roman Empire sometimes treated Syriac Christians as heretics. (b) The Persian Empire persecuted them for a different reason. State it.
questions.a: (a) Some of their beliefs about Christ differed from those of the official Church. (b) Persia suspected them of secretly helping the Romans, its enemies.
s: Part (a): beliefs about Christ differed from the official Church
Part (b): suspected of secretly helping Rome, Persia's enemy

questions.q: (a) Name the empire that fell to Arab Muslim forces in the middle of the 7th century and was home to the Zoroastrians. (b) State any two forms of persecution the Zoroastrians then faced.
questions.a: (a) The Sassanid Empire. (b) Any two of forced conversions to Islam, religious taxes (jizya), destruction of sacred fire temples, social and legal marginalisation.
s: Part (a): the Sassanid Empire
Part (b): two forms of persecution correctly stated

questions.q: Define the terms 'heretic' and 'persecution' as they are used in the chapter.
questions.a: A heretic is a person considered to hold beliefs, especially religious ones, contrary to those of the dominant view. Persecution is hostility, generally arising from religious, ethnic, social or political motives, often accompanied by harassment or violence.
s: Heretic defined as holding beliefs contrary to the dominant view
Persecution defined as hostility with harassment or violence

questions.q: The Parsi sacred fire is still burning. Where, in relation to where the Parsis first arrived, and what does its survival suggest about the community in India?
questions.a: At Udvada, a short distance from where they first arrived in Gujarat. Its survival suggests that the community could keep its ancient traditions alive in India.
s: Udvada, a short distance from the first landing in Gujarat
Survival shows the ancient tradition was kept alive

questions.q: Name two ideas or practices that Zoroastrian thought and the Vedic schools of thought share, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Both have the concept of a cosmic order holding the universe together, and both give much importance to fire worship.
s: Cosmic order holding the universe together
Importance of fire worship

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Devas are beneficial gods in both the Vedas and the Avesta, so the two traditions are the same.' Check his claim against the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. In the Vedas devas are beneficial, but in the Avesta daevas are evil gods who drive towards chaos. The traditions do share cosmic order and fire worship, so they are related but not the same.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Contrast: devas beneficial in the Vedas, daevas evil in the Avesta
Shared ideas such as cosmic order and fire worship show a link, not sameness

questions.q: Retell the Sanjan legend in three steps: what the Raja did, how the Parsi wise man replied, and what the Raja then did.
questions.a: The Raja, unable to speak their language, showed a jug full of milk to say the kingdom was full. A wise man dissolved a spoon of sugar in it without letting it spill. Pleased, the Raja provided a secure place for them to settle.
s: The Raja shows a jug full of milk
The wise man dissolves sugar without spilling
The Raja is pleased and gives a secure place

questions.q: A student writes that the Parsis fled Persia in the 3rd century CE, when the Sassanid Empire began. Show with dates from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The Sassanid Empire lasted from the 3rd to the 7th century and Zoroastrianism was its state religion. The persecution began only after it fell to Arab forces in the middle of the 7th century, and the Parsis reached Gujarat between the 8th and 10th centuries.
s: The empire ran from the 3rd to the 7th century, with Zoroastrianism favoured
Persecution began after the fall in the mid-7th century
Arrival in Gujarat was between the 8th and 10th centuries

questions.q: Compare the reasons for which the Syriac Christians and the Parsis left their homelands and analyse what the two stories show about India.
questions.a: Syriac Christians were treated as heretics by Rome and suspected of helping Rome by Persia, so they travelled east along trade routes to Malabar. The Parsis faced forced conversions, jizya and destruction of fire temples after the Arab conquest, and sailed to Gujarat. Both fled persecution and found a place to live and worship freely, which shows India as a refuge.
s: Syriac Christians: heretics under Rome, suspected under Persia
Parsis: forced conversions, jizya, destroyed fire temples, marginalisation
Analysis: both fled persecution and found freedom to worship in India

questions.q: 'Zoroastrian and Indian traditions are linked by deep spiritual and linguistic ties.' Justify this statement with examples, and name one difference the chapter notes.
questions.a: Spiritually both hold a cosmic order and give importance to fire worship. Linguistically Old Avestan and Vedic Sanskrit share word roots and grammar, for example soma and haoma, hotar and haotar, yajna and yasna. A difference is that devas are beneficial in the Vedas but daevas are evil in the Avesta.
s: Spiritual ties: cosmic order and fire worship
Linguistic ties: shared roots and grammar with two word pairs
One difference: devas versus daevas, or Ahura versus asuras

questions.q:
Dhruv's family from Surat visits Udvada in the holidays. A priest shows them the sacred fire in the 18th-century temple and says the community's forefathers landed close by. Back in school, Dhruv's friend Meher asks him two things: how the Parsis were allowed to stay in a land where the Raja said his kingdom was full, and whether the Parsis kept their identity once they lived in India.
(a) Name the religion of the Parsis and the one God they worship. (b) Which Raja received them, in which kingdom, and what did the Raja show them to say the kingdom was full? (c) Why did the wise man's act of dissolving sugar in the milk without spilling it please the Raja? (d) To answer Meher's second question, Dhruv can use either the burning of the sacred fire at Udvada or the shared word roots of Old Avestan and Vedic Sanskrit. Which is the better evidence, and why?
questions.a: (a) Zoroastrianism; Ahura Mazda. (b) Raja Jadi Rana of Sanjan in coastal Gujarat; a jug full of milk. (c) The sugar sweetened the milk without making it spill, showing that the newcomers would add to the kingdom without crowding anyone out (any sensible reading of the legend). (d) The sacred fire still burning at Udvada is the better evidence, since it shows the community's own tradition surviving in India. The shared word roots show an ancient link between Iran and India, not what the Parsis did after arriving.
s: Part (a): Zoroastrianism and Ahura Mazda
Part (b): Jadi Rana of Sanjan and the jug of milk
Part (c): newcomers would blend in and enrich without displacing others
Part (d): sacred fire at Udvada chosen, with the reason that language roots show ancient ties rather than Parsi identity in India

questions.q:
A history club in Thrissur prepares two cards. Card X is about a community that used an ancient language in worship and was called heretic by one empire and suspected of spying by another. Card Y is about a community that sailed across the Arabian Sea and reached the western coast between the 8th and 10th centuries. A member suggests the line 'Both came to India as traders.'
(a) Identify the communities on Card X and Card Y. (b) Name the coast on which Card X's community settled. (c) Which feature of Card X's journey might make the suggested line sound plausible, and why does it not make them traders? (d) Does the chapter support the line? State the line you would write.
questions.a: (a) X: Syriac Christians; Y: Parsis. (b) The Malabar coast, now Kerala. (c) They travelled along trade routes, but they used the routes to escape persecution, not to trade. (d) No. The chapter says they left to escape persecution; a better line is 'Both came to escape persecution and found freedom to live and worship here.'
s: Part (a): Syriac Christians and Parsis
Part (b): the Malabar coast in Kerala
Part (c): the trade routes they followed, used as a way to escape persecution
Part (d): rejects the line and writes one based on escape from persecution

questions.q: Which building does the chapter call India's oldest mosque, built with the help of early Arab settlers?
questions.a: The Cheraman Juma Masjid in Kerala. Mother Mary Church is an Armenian church in Kolkata, the Lotus Temple is Baha'i, and Bylakuppe is a Tibetan monastery.
o: Cheraman Juma Masjid
Mother Mary Church
Lotus Temple
Bylakuppe monastery

questions.q: Under the Mughals, in which place did the chapter say the earliest Armenian settlement arise, with the emperor's leave to build a church?
questions.a: Agra, where Akbar gave permission. Surat, Kolkata and Chennai are places where Armenians settled later or became influential.
o: Agra
Surat
Kolkata
Chennai

questions.q: Which of these is NOT true of the Arab merchants who came to India from the 7th century, as described in the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says they came as peaceful traders, not as conquerors. Trading spices, marrying local women and becoming part of the Mappila Muslim community are all in the chapter.
o: They came as conquerors to rule the west coast
They traded in spices and other goods
They married local women and formed new communities
In Kerala they became part of the Mappila Muslim community

questions.q: Manav, on a heritage walk in Kolkata, sees an 18th-century college and a church that still function and learns that the city was once a major hub of the community that built them. Which community is it?
questions.a: The Armenians, for whom Kolkata became a major hub with the Armenian College and Mother Mary Church. The Siddis settled in Karnataka and Gujarat, the Parsis centre on Udvada and Gujarat, and the Arab merchants on the west coast.
o: The Armenians
The Siddis
The Parsis
The Arab merchants

questions.q: Neelam in Karnataka watches a troupe dance to African-style drumming and asks why the dancers' ancestors came to India. What does the chapter say?
questions.a: They were brought as enslaved people of Arab, Portuguese and British traders. Coming as spice merchants, fleeing persecution or serving as royal doctors are the stories of other communities.
o: They were brought as slaves of Arab, Portuguese and British traders
They came as merchants to trade in spices along the west coast
They fled religious persecution in their own homelands overseas
They came as doctors and judges to serve the royal court

questions.q:
Read the statements about the communities in this section.
1. The early Arab settlers came to India as peaceful traders, not as conquerors.
2. In the 18th century some Siddis gained prominence in the armies of Muslim rulers.
3. Efforts are being made to give the Siddis better access to education and livelihood options because their overall economic condition has risen above that of most communities.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 is false: efforts are being made for the Siddis' education and livelihoods because their overall economic condition remains poor.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Hirabai Lobi was awarded the Padma Shri in 2023.
Reason (R): The Siddis are designated as a scheduled tribe.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the award was given for her selfless service to her community, not because of the Siddis' scheduled tribe status, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the right description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Abdul Hai  2. Lady Juliana  3. Hirabai Lobi  4. Cheraman Juma Masjid
Column B: a. A doctor in the royal palace  b. Chief Justice in Akbar's court  c. Siddi woman honoured with the Padma Shri  d. India's oldest mosque
questions.a: Abdul Hai was Chief Justice, Lady Juliana a doctor, Hirabai Lobi the Padma Shri awardee and Cheraman Juma Masjid the oldest mosque. The wrong options swap the judge and the doctor, or the awardee and the mosque.

questions.q: (a) Besides trading in spices, name two other things the early Arab merchants did on the west coast. (b) What does this show about how they related to local people?
questions.a: (a) They married local women, formed new communities and helped build the Cheraman Juma Masjid. (b) They mixed with local society and became part of it, as in the Mappila Muslim community.
s: Part (a): two correct activities such as marriage or building the mosque
Part (b): they became part of local society, for example the Mappila community

questions.q: (a) How did the Siddis come to India, and between which centuries? (b) Give one example of how their culture is a fusion of African and Indian traditions.
questions.a: (a) They were enslaved in Africa and brought as slaves of Arab, Portuguese and British traders between the 7th and 19th centuries. (b) Any one: African-style drumming with their dance, or African religious practices combined with Hinduism, Islam or Christianity.
s: Part (a): brought as enslaved people by traders, 7th to 19th centuries
Part (b): one correct example of fusion

questions.q: Who is Hirabai Lobi? State two ways in which she worked for her community.
questions.a: She was a Siddi woman from Gujarat who worked for the upliftment of women of her community. She connected them with banking services and educated them on organic farming and other livelihoods.
s: Identifies her as a Siddi woman from Gujarat
Two ways of serving the community

questions.q: Name two roles Armenians played during the time of the Mughal emperors, giving a named person for one of them.
questions.a: They served in the royal household, the army and the administration. For example, Abdul Hai was Chief Justice in Akbar's court and Lady Juliana was a doctor in the royal palace.
s: Two correct roles
One named person with the role

questions.q: The chapter calls the Siddis' story 'a different kind of story' from that of the Arab merchants. Explain what is different in how each group came to India.
questions.a: The Arab merchants came as traders, not as conquerors, and settled. The Siddis were enslaved in Africa and brought as slaves of traders.
s: Arab merchants came as peaceful traders, not conquerors
Siddis were enslaved and brought as slaves

questions.q: Tara says, 'Every community in this section came to India to escape persecution.' Test her claim with the Arab merchants, the Siddis and the Armenians.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Arab merchants came to trade, the Siddis were brought as enslaved people, and the Armenians came as merchants and gained patronage and prosperity. 'Every' is too strong; one counter-example is enough.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong because of the word 'every'
Arab merchants came to trade and the Siddis were brought as slaves
Armenians came as merchants and gained patronage or prosperity (not escape from persecution)

questions.q: Describe how the Armenians became a part of Chennai's life, using three points from the chapter.
questions.a: Armenian merchants settled in Madras around the mid-17th century and became influential in commerce, dealing in silk, spices and precious stones. Armenian Street in George Town and St. Mary's Armenian Church from the mid-18th century keep their memory alive.
s: Settled around the mid-17th century
Dealt in silk, spices and precious stones
Armenian Street and the church as lasting marks

questions.q: Write three quiz clues, each using a fact from the chapter, so that the answer to the full quiz question is 'the Siddis'.
questions.a: Any three accurate clues, for example: they are of African origin; they have a distinctive dance with African-style drumming; they are designated a scheduled tribe.
s: Clue 1 is accurate and from the chapter
Clue 2 is accurate and different
Clue 3 is accurate and the three together point only to the Siddis

questions.q: Compare the Arab merchants and the Siddis on how they came to India, what they did here and how their identity developed.
questions.a: The Arab merchants came from the 7th century as peaceful traders, traded spices, married local women and became part of the Mappila Muslim community. The Siddis were enslaved in Africa and brought between the 7th and 19th centuries; some rose in armies in the 18th century. Their identity fuses African and Indian traditions.
s: How the Arab merchants came
How the Siddis came
What the Arab merchants did and became
What the Siddis did and how their identity developed

questions.q: 'The Armenians left a lasting cultural impact on India's cities.' Justify this with evidence from Agra, Kolkata and Chennai.
questions.a: In Agra, Akbar let them build a church, and Armenians served the Mughal household, army and administration. In Kolkata, the 18th-century Armenian College and Mother Mary Church are still active. In Chennai, Armenian Street and St. Mary's Armenian Church recall their influence in trade.
s: Agra: church permitted by Akbar and roles in the Mughal court
Kolkata: Armenian College and Mother Mary Church still active
Chennai: trade influence, Armenian Street and the church

questions.q:
Mukta, a Class 7 student in Gujarat, reads about a woman of African descent who settled in her state, helped women of her community with banking and organic farming, and was honoured nationally in 2023. Her school wants its 'Community Week' to leave the community she belongs to better off, not merely better known. Two plans are proposed. Plan X: an evening where community artists perform their own dance with drumming. Plan Y: a fund for books and fees for children of the community.
(a) Name the woman, her community and the honour. (b) How did her community come to India? (c) What does the chapter say about the community's overall economic condition, and what efforts are being made? (d) Which plan, X or Y, better meets the school's stated aim, and what does the other plan do well instead? Justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Hirabai Lobi, the Siddi community, the Padma Shri. (b) Brought as slaves of Arab, Portuguese and British traders. (c) Overall economic condition remains poor; efforts are being made to give better access to education and livelihood options. (d) Plan Y meets the aim of leaving the community better off, since it matches the chapter's efforts on education. Plan X celebrates the distinctive dance and African-style drumming that make their identity a fusion of African and Indian traditions, so it makes the community better known rather than better off.
s: Part (a): Hirabai Lobi, Siddi, Padma Shri
Part (b): brought as slaves of traders
Part (c): condition remains poor; efforts for education and livelihood
Part (d): Plan Y chosen using (c), with the strength of Plan X (cultural identity) stated

questions.q:
Students from Chennai walk down a lane in George Town named after a merchant community of centuries ago. At its end stands a church built in the mid-18th century. The guide says only a handful of families now remain. The group argues over whether the community should be called 'vanished' or 'part of the city's heritage'.
(a) Name the community and the church. (b) State which goods they traded and when they settled in Madras. (c) In which other two cities, besides Madras and Agra, did they settle? (d) Judge which description, 'vanished' or 'part of the heritage', the chapter supports better.
questions.a: (a) Armenians; St. Mary's Armenian Church. (b) Silk, spices and precious stones; around the mid-17th century. (c) Surat and Kolkata. (d) Heritage: although the population has dwindled, a handful of families and heritage groups preserve their architecture, trade and spiritual legacy.
s: Part (a): Armenians and St. Mary's Armenian Church
Part (b): silk, spices, precious stones; mid-17th century
Part (c): Surat and Kolkata
Part (d): heritage, justified by the surviving families and legacy

questions.q: Who led the new religion that began in mid-19th-century Persia and spoke of unity among all people?
questions.a: Baha'u'llah. Zarathushtra founded Zoroastrianism, Digvijaysinhji was the Maharaja of Nawanagar, and the 14th Dalai Lama is the Tibetan leader who took refuge in India.
o: Baha'u'llah
Zarathushtra
Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji
The 14th Dalai Lama

questions.q: The Lotus Temple in New Delhi is a place of worship of which community?
questions.a: The Baha'is. A synagogue belongs to the Jews, a fire temple to the Parsis, and a monastery such as Bylakuppe to Tibetan Buddhists.
o: The Baha'is
The Jews
The Parsis
The Tibetan Buddhists

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the chapter about the Maharaja of Nawanagar and the Polish children?
questions.a: The chapter says the children and others returned home safely after the war, so permanent adoption is false. The Red Cross appeal, the figure of about a thousand orphans and the food and care are all in the chapter.
o: The orphans were adopted and never returned to Poland
He mobilised the Red Cross and other organisations
He saved around a thousand orphans between 1942 and 1946
He gave the children a safe place, food and care

questions.q: To which place were the rescued Polish children taken by the Maharaja?
questions.a: To Jamnagar, in Nawanagar State. Travancore is the kingdom around Kochi, Sanjan is where the Parsis were received, and Dharamshala is where the Tibetan administration functions.
o: Jamnagar, in Nawanagar State
Kochi, in the kingdom of Travancore
Sanjan, in coastal Gujarat
Dharamshala, in Himachal Pradesh

questions.q: Tomasz, a tourist standing in Good Maharaja Square in Warsaw, asks why a ruler from India is honoured there. What does the chapter say the monument recognises?
questions.a: His help to Polish refugees during the Second World War. The Kochi land grant belongs to the Jewish story, the Syriac Christians' journey was along trade routes, and the Dalai Lama's asylum in 1959 is the Tibetan story.
o: His help to Polish refugees during the Second World War
His grant of land to the Jews of Kochi
His welcome to Syriac Christians reaching the Malabar coast
His asylum to the Dalai Lama in 1959

questions.q: At a prayer hall in New Delhi, an Iranian-born visitor says her ancestors left Iran because their leaders called them heretics. Which belief of her community does the chapter give?
questions.a: Unity among all people and harmony between religions. The worship of Ahura Mazda is Zoroastrian, the prayer remembered by the Bene Israel is Jewish, and the Four Commitments are the Dalai Lama's.
o: Unity among all people and harmony between religions
Worship of one God, Ahura Mazda, and choosing good over evil
A prayer saying there is only one God, remembered despite lost books
Promotion of human values, religious harmony and Tibetan culture

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Baha'i community.
1. The Baha'i religion began in India in the mid-1800s.
2. Today every Baha'i living in India is an Iranian who arrived recently.
3. The Baha'is welcome people of all religions and backgrounds.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 3 is correct. The religion began in Persia, and the chapter says that most Baha'is in India today are Indians who believe in the faith's message of unity and love.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A monument to the Maharaja of Nawanagar stands in Warsaw.
Reason (R): He rescued around a thousand Polish orphans between 1942 and 1946 and welcomed thousands of Polish refugees.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and his rescue of the Polish children and refugees is why Poland honoured him, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Why did Iran's ruling religious leadership brand the Baha'is as heretics? (b) How did this lead some Baha'is to India, and who forms most of the Baha'i community in India today?
questions.a: (a) Because their beliefs were different. (b) Some looked for safer places and India was one of the first they came to, from the late 19th century. Most Baha'is in India today are Indians.
s: Part (a): their beliefs were different from those of the ruling leadership
Part (b): they sought safety in India, and most Baha'is here today are Indians

questions.q: (a) Name the war during which Poland was invaded and give its years. (b) What happened to many Polish children, and what did the Maharaja do in response?
questions.a: (a) The Second World War, 1939 to 1945. (b) Many children were orphaned; he mobilised the Red Cross and other organisations, took the children to Jamnagar and gave them a safe place, food and care.
s: Part (a): the Second World War, 1939 to 1945
Part (b): the orphaned children and the Maharaja's rescue and care

questions.q: State the two main teachings of the Baha'i faith as given in the chapter.
questions.a: Unity among all people and harmony between religions.
s: Unity among all people
Harmony between religions

questions.q: Where is the Good Maharaja Square, and who recognised the Maharaja's service in the early 21st century?
questions.a: The Good Maharaja Square is in Warsaw, Poland, and the President of Poland recognised his service, after which the monument was built.
s: Warsaw, Poland
The President of Poland recognised the service

questions.q: The chapter says India was 'a home away from home, even if for a brief period' for the Polish orphans. (a) What made it a 'home'? (b) Besides the orphans, whom else did the Maharaja welcome?
questions.a: (a) A safe place to stay, food to eat and care. (b) Several thousand Polish refugees fleeing from other areas, who were welcomed to stay in the safety of his state.
s: A safe place, food and care made it a home
Several thousand Polish refugees fleeing from other areas

questions.q: Gauri says, 'Only the people of Nawanagar remembered the Maharaja's rescue of the Polish children; Poland never honoured him.' Check her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. In the early 21st century the President of Poland recognised his service and a monument was built in his honour in Good Maharaja Square, Warsaw. 'Never' and 'only' are too strong.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong, with 'never' and 'only' challenged
Evidence: the President of Poland recognised his service in the early 21st century
Evidence: a monument in Warsaw's Good Maharaja Square was built in his honour

questions.q: Compare the Baha'i story and the Polish children's story in three points: what danger each group faced, what India offered, and what happened afterwards.
questions.a: The Baha'is were branded heretics and treated badly in Iran; the Polish children were orphaned by war. India gave both a safe place. Many Indians joined the Baha'i faith and most Baha'is in India are now Indians, while the Polish children returned home after the war.
s: Danger: persecution in Iran versus war in Poland
India offered safety to both
Afterwards: the Baha'is stayed and grew, the Poles returned home

questions.q: A student writes that the Maharaja's rescue of the Polish orphans began in 1946, after the war was over. Use dates from the chapter to show this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter gives the rescue as 1942 to 1946, so it began in 1942, while the war (1939 to 1945) was still going on. It ended in 1946, so 1946 is the end of the rescue, not the start.
s: The war ran from 1939 to 1945
The chapter gives the rescue years as 1942 to 1946, so it began in 1942
1942 falls during the war, and 1946 is the end year of the rescue, not the start

questions.q: 'The Maharaja of Nawanagar turned a tragedy of war into a story of shelter.' Justify this with details from the chapter.
questions.a: Poland was invaded in the Second World War; families were torn apart and many children orphaned. The Maharaja mobilised the Red Cross and other organisations, took the children to Jamnagar and provided a safe place, food and care. He saved around a thousand orphans between 1942 and 1946, and welcomed several thousand refugees. His service was honoured by the President of Poland and a monument in Warsaw.
s: The tragedy: invasion, torn families and orphans
His actions: Red Cross, Jamnagar, safe place, food and care
The scale: about a thousand orphans and thousands of refugees
The recognition in Poland

questions.q: Compare the Baha'is and the Polish orphans on why they came to India and how long they stayed, and analyse what each story shows about India.
questions.a: The Baha'is came from Persia in the late 19th century because they were treated badly as heretics; the Polish orphans came during the war of 1939-1945. The Baha'is stayed and many Indians joined the faith, while the Poles returned after the war. The first shows India as a long-term home and the second as a safe shelter in a crisis.
s: Baha'is: treated badly as heretics, arrived late 19th century
Polish orphans: came during the war of 1939 to 1945
Stay: Baha'is stayed and many Indians joined, Poles returned home
Analysis: India as a lasting home in one case and a safe shelter in a crisis in the other

questions.q:
During a school exchange, a Polish student visits a Jamnagar school and lays flowers at a plaque for a former ruler. Indian students are asked to prepare a plaque that proves why a square in Warsaw calls him the 'Good Maharaja'. The plaque must prove he deserved the title without relying on anyone else's opinion of him.
(a) Name the ruler and the state he ruled. (b) Which organisations did he mobilise, what did he provide the children, and about how many orphans did he save? (c) What did Poland do in the early 21st century, and who did it? (d) For the plaque, which is the stronger proof of the title, the facts in (b) or the facts in (c)? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, Nawanagar State. (b) The Red Cross and other organisations; a safe place, food and care; around a thousand orphans. (c) The President of Poland recognised his service and a monument was built in Warsaw. (d) The facts in (b): they are what he himself did, whereas (c) is Poland's opinion, given later because of (b). (c) is useful only as supporting evidence.
s: Part (a): the Maharaja of Nawanagar
Part (b): Red Cross and others; safe place, food, care; about a thousand orphans
Part (c): the President of Poland recognised him and a monument was built
Part (d): (b) chosen as the stronger proof because it is his own action and (c) rests on others' recognition

questions.q:
Saira's class visits the Lotus Temple in New Delhi, which welcomes visitors of all religions. The guide says the community that prays there began in Persia and was once treated badly at home. A student asks, 'Did these people come to India by chance?'
(a) Name the founder of the faith and the century of its beginning. (b) Why were its followers treated badly in Iran? (c) When did Baha'is start arriving in India, and what were they looking for? (d) For a poster, which is the better evidence that the faith has become part of India: that Iranian Baha'is arrived in the late 19th century, or that many Indians joined and most Baha'is in India are Indians? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Baha'u'llah, the mid-1800s. (b) The ruling religious leadership branded them heretics because of their different beliefs. (c) From the late 19th century, looking for safer places to live. (d) That many Indians joined and most Baha'is here are Indians is better evidence: the arrival of Iranians only shows when the faith came, while Indians joining shows it took root in India.
s: Part (a): Baha'u'llah, mid-19th century
Part (b): branded heretics for different beliefs
Part (c): late 19th century; looking for safer places
Part (d): Indians joining chosen, with the reason that arrival shows only when the faith came

questions.q: In which year, after a popular uprising in Lhasa, did the 14th Dalai Lama flee to India?
questions.a: In 1959. The year 1950 is when China began overrunning Tibet, 1946 is the year the rescue of Polish children ended, and 1893 is the year of Swami Vivekananda's speech.

questions.q: From which Indian town does the Central Tibetan Administration function as a government-in-exile?
questions.a: Dharamshala in Himachal Pradesh. Bylakuppe is a monastery settlement in Karnataka, Lhasa is Tibet's own former capital, and Goa has only a Tibetan market in the chapter.
o: Dharamshala
Bylakuppe
Lhasa
Goa

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Dalai Lama's Four Commitments?
questions.a: Reviving a medical council is not a commitment; Sowa Rigpa is a medical tradition. The other three are among the four named in the chapter.
o: Reviving the Sowa Rigpa medical council
Promoting human values like compassion, forgiveness and tolerance
Promoting religious harmony
Preserving Tibetan culture

questions.q: A clinic in Dharamshala treats chronic diseases using a system said to have been codified in the 8th century by a medical council held near Lhasa. Which system is it?
questions.a: Sowa Rigpa, the 'Art of Healing'. Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha are other AYUSH systems, but they were not codified by a council near Lhasa.
o: Sowa Rigpa
Ayurveda
Unani
Siddha

questions.q: Meera visits a monastery in Karnataka that looks like the original ones in Tibet. According to the chapter, why were such monasteries established in India?
questions.a: They gave Tibetan Buddhists a space to follow their way of life and spiritual practices without fear or hindrance. The administration functions from Dharamshala, and the Dalai Lamas ruled in Tibet.
o: To let Tibetan Buddhists pursue their way of life without fear or hindrance
To house the Central Tibetan Administration that works in exile
To keep safe the Sanskrit manuscripts that were brought from Nalanda
To train the Dalai Lama so that he can rule Tibet as a king

questions.q:
Read the statements about Tibet and India.
1. In the 7th century Tibet became a centre of Buddhism when its king embraced the Buddha's teachings.
2. After the destruction of Nalanda and other centres of learning, many monks left for Tibet, often taking Sanskrit manuscripts.
3. From the mid-17th century the Dalai Lamas became the rulers of Tibet.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are from the chapter.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Sowa Rigpa has been integrated into the Government of India's AYUSH programme.
Reason (R): Tibet is India's northern neighbour, on the other side of the Himalayan range.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but Tibet's location says nothing about why its medicine joined AYUSH, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Men-Tsee-Khang  2. Bylakuppe  3. Dharamshala  4. Sowa Rigpa
Column B: a. Home of the government-in-exile  b. Tibetan monastery in Karnataka  c. Institution that practises Tibetan medicine  d. 'Art of Healing' codified near Lhasa
questions.a: Men-Tsee-Khang practises Tibetan medicine, Bylakuppe is the Karnataka monastery, Dharamshala houses the Central Tibetan Administration and Sowa Rigpa is the 'Art of Healing'. Wrong options swap the place with the institution or the system.

questions.q: (a) Why did many monks leave eastern India for Tibet in the 12th and 13th centuries? (b) What did they often take with them?
questions.a: (a) Turko-Afghan military invasions in eastern India destroyed Nalanda and other Buddhist centres of learning. (b) Precious manuscripts of Sanskrit texts.
s: Part (a): the destruction of Nalanda and other centres of learning
Part (b): Sanskrit manuscripts

questions.q: (a) What happened in Lhasa in 1959? (b) How did this lead the 14th Dalai Lama to India, and what did the Indian government grant him?
questions.a: (a) A popular uprising against the Chinese presence. (b) He was advised to flee across the Himalaya and India granted him asylum.
s: Part (a): popular uprising against the Chinese presence
Part (b): fled across the Himalaya and was granted asylum

questions.q: What is Sowa Rigpa? Name the Government of India programme in which it has been integrated.
questions.a: It is the traditional Tibetan system of medicine, also called the 'Art of Healing', codified in the 8th century CE. It is part of the AYUSH programme.
s: Sowa Rigpa as the Tibetan system of medicine
The AYUSH programme

questions.q: State any two of the Dalai Lama's Four Commitments, and give one example of the values named under the commitment on human values.
questions.a: Any two of promoting human values, promoting religious harmony, preserving Tibetan culture, and reviving India's civilisational heritage. Human values include compassion, forgiveness and tolerance.
s: Two commitments correctly stated
One example such as compassion, forgiveness or tolerance

questions.q: From which century did the Dalai Lamas begin to assume a greater role in Tibet, and from when were they Tibet's rulers? Say how each Dalai Lama was believed to be related to the one before.
questions.a: From the 15th century onward they assumed a greater role, becoming spiritual heads and, from the mid-17th century, Tibet's rulers. Each was said to be the reincarnation of his predecessor.
s: 15th century onward: greater role; mid-17th century: rulers
Each Dalai Lama said to be his predecessor's reincarnation

questions.q: Nisha says, 'The Dalai Lama's Four Commitments are only about Tibet and have nothing to do with India.' Evaluate her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Two commitments are about values for everyone (human values like compassion, forgiveness and tolerance, and religious harmony). The fourth is the revival of India's civilisational heritage, particularly karuna (compassion) and ahimsa (nonviolence). Only one commitment, the preservation of Tibetan culture, is specifically Tibetan.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong because of 'only' and 'nothing'
Evidence: the fourth commitment is the revival of India's civilisational heritage
Names the Indian values karuna and ahimsa, and notes that only one commitment is specifically Tibetan

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'Dharamshala'. Write three clues, each using a different fact from the chapter, so that together they point only to Dharamshala.
questions.a: Any three accurate clues, for example: the 14th Dalai Lama lives here as an 'honoured guest'; the Central Tibetan Administration functions here as a government-in-exile; it is in Himachal Pradesh; Men-Tsee-Khang here practises Tibetan medicine.
s: Clue 1 is accurate and from the chapter
Clue 2 is accurate and different
Clue 3 is accurate and the three together point only to Dharamshala

questions.q: Explain how Sowa Rigpa shows that Tibetan medicine drew on many places, and how it reached a place in India's own systems.
questions.a: Sowa Rigpa blends ancient principles of Ayurveda with inputs from China, Central Asia, Persia and even Greece. It was codified near Lhasa in the 8th century, was propagated by Tibetans in India after 1959 and is now part of the AYUSH programme.
s: Blend of Ayurveda with inputs from China, Central Asia, Persia and even Greece
Codified in the 8th century by a medical council near Lhasa
Propagated by Tibetans in India after 1959 and integrated into the AYUSH programme

questions.q: 'Tibetan refugees have become part of Indian society while keeping their own heritage.' Justify this with evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: The government rehabilitated them, educated their children and facilitated settlements to preserve language, culture and heritage. Monasteries patterned on the originals let them pursue their way of life without fear. Non-government organisations provided livelihoods. Sowa Rigpa is practised at Men-Tsee-Khang and is part of AYUSH.
s: Government measures: rehabilitation, education, settlements
Monasteries allowing spiritual practice without fear
NGO livelihood support
Sowa Rigpa and AYUSH as heritage contributing to India

questions.q: Trace the links between India and Tibet from the 7th century to 1959, and analyse why India was a natural place of refuge for the Dalai Lama.
questions.a: In the 7th century Tibet became a centre of Buddhism. After Nalanda was destroyed, monks took Sanskrit manuscripts to Tibet. From the 15th century the Dalai Lamas gained a greater role and ruled from the mid-17th century. In 1950 China began overrunning Tibet and in 1959, after the Lhasa uprising, the Dalai Lama fled across the Himalaya. India, Tibet's northern neighbour and the source of the Nalanda manuscripts, granted him asylum.
s: 7th century: Tibet becomes a centre of Buddhism
12th and 13th centuries: monks take Sanskrit manuscripts after Nalanda
Dalai Lamas' role from the 15th century and 1950 to 1959 events
Analysis: Tibet is India's northern neighbour, the Nalanda link, and India granted asylum in 1959

questions.q:
Pema's school in Bengaluru visits a Tibetan monastery in Karnataka. A monk says the building is patterned on the original ones in Tibet. A visitor remarks that Tibetans had no link with India before 1959. A donor wants to help young Tibetans who are already settled in Indian towns to earn their own living, and offers to fund either a new monastery or a livelihood programme.
(a) Why were such monasteries created in India? (b) Which kind of organisation has supported the community by providing livelihood options? (c) Correct the visitor with a link between India and Tibet that is older than 1959. (d) Which gift better meets the donor's aim, and what does the other gift do well instead? Justify with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) To create a space for Tibetan Buddhists to pursue their way of life and spiritual practices without fear or hindrance. (b) Non-government organisations. (c) Monks took Sanskrit manuscripts from Nalanda to Tibet in the 12th-13th centuries, or Tibet became a centre of Buddhism in the 7th century. (d) The livelihood programme meets the aim of earning a living, as NGOs have done for the community. The monastery preserves spiritual life and culture rather than income.
s: Part (a): a space to pursue their way of life and spiritual practices without fear
Part (b): non-government organisations
Part (c): an older link such as the Nalanda manuscripts
Part (d): livelihood programme chosen for the stated aim, and the monastery's strength (spiritual life, culture) named

questions.q:
After an uprising in Lhasa against the Chinese presence, a senior religious leader is advised to flee across the Himalaya. A Class 7 group in Shimla plans a display about him. The display must show Tibetans reviving India's own heritage, and there is room for either his Four Commitments or the story of Tibetan medicine.
(a) Name the leader and the Indian town where he lives. (b) What phrase describes his position in India, and which administration functions from there? (c) Which of his Four Commitments is about India itself, and which two Indian values does it name? (d) Choose the Four Commitments or Tibetan medicine for the display, and justify with the stated aim.
questions.a: (a) The 14th Dalai Lama; Dharamshala. (b) An 'honoured guest'; the Central Tibetan Administration as a government-in-exile. (c) The revival of India's civilisational heritage; karuna (compassion) and ahimsa (nonviolence). (d) The Four Commitments: the fourth directly names reviving India's own values. Tibetan medicine shows a Tibetan tradition that blends Ayurveda and joined AYUSH, which shows contribution but not the revival of India's heritage itself.
s: Part (a): the 14th Dalai Lama and Dharamshala
Part (b): honoured guest and the Central Tibetan Administration
Part (c): the revival of India's civilisational heritage; karuna and ahimsa
Part (d): Four Commitments chosen, using the stated aim and the fourth commitment

questions.q: What does the phrase 'vasudhaiva kutumbakam' mean, as given in the chapter?
questions.a: The whole world is family. 'May all creatures be happy' is sarve bhavantu sukhinah, 'a guest is like God' is atithi devo bhava, and 'this is mine, that is not mine' is the narrow-minded view.
o: The whole world is family
May all creatures be happy
A guest is like God
This is mine, that is not mine

questions.q: Which text does the chapter quote to express 'loving-kindness', comparing it to a mother protecting her only child?
questions.a: The Karaniya Metta Sutta, the Buddha's words on loving-kindness. The Hitopadesha is the source of the opening verse, and the Avesta and the Torah belong to the Parsi and Jewish traditions.
o: The Karaniya Metta Sutta
The Hitopadesha
The Avesta
The Torah

questions.q: Which of the following does the chapter NOT say about Indian communities living abroad?
questions.a: The chapter says they are perceived as peaceful, law-abiding, progressive and prosperous, so a quarrelsome minority that avoids local society is false. The other three statements are in the chapter.
o: They are seen as a quarrelsome minority that avoids local society
They are perceived as peaceful and law-abiding people overseas
They contribute to the economy of the country where they live
They integrate well in the society of that country they join

questions.q: According to the 'Before we move on' summary, what have India's values of inclusion enabled even small communities to do?
questions.a: Find India a secure place and maintain their traditions over centuries. Taking over the government, avoiding cities or giving up their languages are not stated.
o: Find a secure place and keep their traditions over centuries
Take a share in the government of the country
Give up their languages and customs to join the local culture
Settle only in the cities and avoid villages

questions.q: A quiz card reads: 'These rulers came intending to conquer India but were won over by its diverse culture, rich philosophy and thriving economy.' Which pair does the chapter name?
questions.a: The Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas, whom the chapter recalls from Part 1. The other pairs are communities that came as refugees or merchants, not as would-be conquerors.
o: The Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas
The Bene Israel and the Parsis
The Armenians and the Siddis
The Arab merchants and the Baha'is

questions.q: After a flood, the volunteers of a Nagpur school feed every hungry person and stray animal in the relief camp, not only their own neighbours, wishing every living being to be well. Which value from the chapter are they following?
questions.a: Sarve bhavantu sukhinah, 'may all creatures be happy', since the volunteers care for every living being. Atithi devo bhava is about honouring a guest, vasudhaiva kutumbakam says the whole world is family, and ahimsa is non-violence.
o: Sarve bhavantu sukhinah
Atithi devo bhava
Vasudhaiva kutumbakam
Ahimsa

questions.q:
Read the statements from the chapter's closing section.
1. The idea of 'the whole world is family' is described as not just a slogan but a practice for millennia.
2. The Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas are the only people who came to conquer India and were conquered by its culture; there are no other cases.
3. The idea of the fundamental unity of humankind is a core civilisational value of India that can help the world face crises such as wars, climate change and inequality.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says there are many such cases and 'there are more'.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India has been a haven for people persecuted in their homelands.
Reason (R): India developed a culture of peaceful coexistence and acceptance of various faiths and schools of thought.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and the culture of acceptance is the reason persecuted people found India secure, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Give the meaning of 'sarve bhavantu sukhinah' and of 'atithi devo bhava'. (b) A shopkeeper in Hyderabad gives a hungry traveller who reaches his door a meal and a place to rest. Which of the two is he following, and why?
questions.a: (a) 'May all creatures be happy' and 'a guest is like God'. (b) Atithi devo bhava, because he treats the traveller who has arrived as a guest to be honoured.
s: Part (a): both meanings correctly given
Part (b): atithi devo bhava, with the reason of treating the arrival as a guest

questions.q: (a) Name two qualities for which a sizeable Indian community abroad is perceived. (b) Why does the chapter find this 'striking', in the light of the values it has discussed?
questions.a: (a) Any two of peaceful, law-abiding, progressive and prosperous. (b) Because the Indian expatriate community has carried and practised similar values abroad, integrating well and contributing to the economy.
s: Part (a): two qualities named
Part (b): the same values are carried and practised abroad

questions.q: What comparison does the Karaniya Metta Sutta use, and what attitude towards all living beings does it recommend?
questions.a: It compares the attitude to a mother who protects her only child with her life. It recommends cherishing all living beings with a boundless heart and radiating kindness over the entire world.
s: The mother and her only child comparison
Boundless kindness towards all living beings

questions.q: Name the two peoples the chapter gives as examples of those who came intending to conquer India, and say what happened to them in India.
questions.a: The Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas; they were conquered instead by India's diverse culture, rich philosophy and knowledge traditions, unique geography and climate, and thriving economy.
s: Indo-Greeks and Kushanas
They were conquered by India's culture, philosophy, geography or economy instead

questions.q: The chapter says vasudhaiva kutumbakam is 'not just a slogan but has been a practice for millennia'. Which evidence from the chapter's stories supports 'practice', and why does that matter?
questions.a: The communities that made India their home, such as the Jews at Kochi, the Parsis in Gujarat or the Tibetans in Dharamshala, were given a place to live. That shows the idea was acted on, not only spoken.
s: Names communities that were given a place
Explains that this shows the idea was acted on and not only spoken

questions.q: Ishaan says, 'India welcomed outsiders only because they brought wealth and trade.' Evaluate his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Many came seeking refuge from persecution, such as Jews, Syriac Christians, Parsis, Baha'is and Tibetans, and the chapter credits Indian values such as vasudhaiva kutumbakam and atithi devo bhava. Some did come for opportunity, but not only.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong because of 'only'
Many came as refugees from persecution
Indian values of welcome are given as the basis

questions.q: The opening verse says narrow-minded people think 'this is mine, that is not mine', and Sri Sarada Devi says 'No one is a stranger, my child'. Explain how both express the chapter's central idea.
questions.a: The verse contrasts the narrow-minded, who divide people into mine and not mine, with the noble-minded, for whom the whole world is family. Sri Sarada Devi tells a child that no one is a stranger and the whole world is your own. Both express vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the basis of India's welcome.
s: The verse contrasts narrow-minded and noble-minded views
Sarada Devi's message that no one is a stranger
Both express the idea that the whole world is family

questions.q: Create a short school situation in which a student could act on 'vasudhaiva kutumbakam'. State the setting, the action, and how it fits the idea.
questions.a: Any situation that fits, for example: a new student from another country joins Class 7 mid-year; classmates invite her to sit with them and share their lunch; this treats her as part of the family, not as a stranger.
s: A realistic school setting
A clear action that shows welcome
Links the action to the idea that the whole world is family

questions.q: 'Indian values created a haven for the persecuted.' Justify this by naming three values from the chapter and showing how they were put into practice for three communities.
questions.a: The values are vasudhaiva kutumbakam, atithi devo bhava and sarve bhavantu sukhinah, with compassion in the Karaniya Metta Sutta. In practice, the Raja of Kochi gave Jews land free of cost, Raja Jadi Rana gave the Parsis a secure place at Sanjan, and India granted the Dalai Lama asylum and rehabilitated Tibetan refugees.
s: Three values named with their meanings
Three communities and how each was received
Links the practices to the culture of acceptance

questions.q: Name the idea the chapter calls a core civilisational value of India and the crises it says it can help the world resolve, and give three pieces of evidence from the chapter that support calling it a core value.
questions.a: The fundamental unity of humankind can help resolve wars, climate change, increasing inequality and discrimination. Evidence: ideas such as sarve bhavantu sukhinah, atithi devo bhava and vasudhaiva kutumbakam, practised for millennia; the Karaniya Metta Sutta's loving-kindness; and the stories of communities sheltered in India.
s: Names the idea and the crises it can help resolve
Three pieces of chapter evidence, one mark each, with the third also linked to the idea

questions.q:
The student council of a Hyderabad school plans a 'Many Homes, One Family' week. Its aim is to show that vasudhaiva kutumbakam is 'not just a slogan but has been a practice for millennia'. One poster says that narrow-minded people think 'this is mine, that is not mine', while for the noble-minded the whole world is family. A second shows an Indian family settled abroad and respected there. A third shows rulers who came to conquer India and stayed. The council must choose one poster to open the assembly.
(a) Name the idea stated on the first poster. (b) How are Indian communities abroad perceived, according to the chapter? (c) Name two groups the third poster may show and say what became of them in India. (d) Which poster best meets the council's aim, and why do the others fall short?
questions.a: (a) Vasudhaiva kutumbakam, the whole world is family. (b) As peaceful, law-abiding, progressive and prosperous, contributing to the economy and integrating well. (c) The Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas, who were conquered by India's culture. (d) The third poster: it shows the idea acted on within India. The first states the idea but is only words, and the second shows Indian values practised abroad, not India's own welcome.
s: Part (a): vasudhaiva kutumbakam
Part (b): peaceful, law-abiding, progressive and prosperous
Part (c): Indo-Greeks and Kushanas, conquered by India's culture
Part (d): third poster chosen with reasons that the first is only words and the second is about abroad

questions.q:
Isha's grandmother says: 'When a stranger knocked on a rainy night, my mother made room and gave him tea; a guest, she said, is like God.' Isha's class has debated the chapter's midnight stranger scenario and is split: half say safety first, half say help first. The teacher asks them to connect the story to the chapter.
(a) Which value does the grandmother's saying express? (b) Name one more value from the chapter that points the same way. (c) Which one story from the chapter shows this value being practised for a community? (d) Give one argument for and one against sheltering the stranger, and say which side the chapter's stories favour.
questions.a: (a) Atithi devo bhava. (b) Vasudhaiva kutumbakam, sarve bhavantu sukhinah or compassion. (c) For example, the Raja of Kochi gave land to the Jews, or the Maharaja of Nawanagar sheltered Polish children. (d) For: compassion and the guest being like God; against: unknown risk to the family. The stories favour shelter, as India repeatedly welcomed the persecuted.
s: Part (a): atithi devo bhava
Part (b): another value correctly named
Part (c): a community story that shows welcome
Part (d): one argument each side and a justified lean toward shelter
